Mr. Chairman, I wish to raise a few points in this afternoon's debate.
I concur in the remarks of the hon. member for Roberval, who has just spoken, about the complications that arise through the operation of the three year waiting period under the retraining scheme. I think of the older person who returns to the ordinary, academic school to improve his academic qualifications, graduates, and then finds that he cannot apply for assistance which would be most useful to him in retraining as he has not been in the labour force for three years. That sort of situation can create real difficulties. The hon. member who spoke before me went into this matter in greater detail than I shall.
With respect to the various aspects of immigration, I think all members of the house support the new regulations which allow for a wider range of immigrants and for easier entry into this country, though in the area of sponsored immigrants some interesting factors develop. May I quote from page 4 of newsletter No. 3 which deals with the new selection policy for immigration.
We feel that the relative of a Canadian or of a landed immigrant, coming to Canada as a worker, should have precedence over other workers and should be admissible with fewer qualifications than are required of independent immigrants ...
The greatest preference in this type of immigration would be given to sons and daughters, parents and grandparents who do not qualify as dependents, brothers and sisters and nephews and nieces under 21, if sponsored by a citizen...
We would also propose to extend the sponsorship privilege to cover nephews and nieces over 21, uncles and aunts and grandchildren. These relatives would not be admitted as freely as the first group but would need lower qualifications than an independent immigrant.
We see a genuine sliding scale in the regulations. The point I wish to bring to the minister's attention has to do with the closeness of family relationships. One factor has been overlooked in the regulations, the factor of the Canadian who has no living relative in Canada but has a living relative outside Canada. I am talking of a Canadian with resources at his disposal to establish such a relative in this country. It seems to me that each Canadian ought to have a basic right to sponsor somebody at some time. We allow some Canadians to sponsor many people for entry into this country. Yet a Canadian who may have been born here and has made a great contribution to Canada and built up a

Supply-Manpower and Immigration personal fortune may find that he cannot sponsor relatives from outside the country because they fall outside the list that is included in the regulations. As a result he is frustrated in obtaining the admission of his relative because that relative does not fall within the closely related group. Nevertheless, since the Canadian has no other relative his relationship with the relative outside Canada may be as close as his relationship would have been with a brother, sister, father or any of those who receive better treatment under the regulations.
I am concerned about the minister's drive to bring French speaking immigrants to Canada. Somehow I feel that we should not become involved in the numbers game with respect to this area of division within the country. The minister's effort is worthy and I do not think many Canadians would not welcome immigrants from France, Switzerland and Belgium. But I very much doubt that there should be specific latitude for French speaking vis-a-vis English speaking immigrants. The minister is rowing a leaky boat in this regard.
The governments of Switzerland and Belgium are concerned about the increasing use of the English language within their countries. Because of language difficulties which have arisen in both countries English has become very much the second language. We might obtain quite a number of immigrants from those countries without obtaining the balance, or imbalance, which may have been in the minister's mind with respect to French speaking immigrants when he gave us the figures this afternoon.
We can learn something about immigration from Switzerland where, though one-sixth of the labour force comes from outside the country, the economy seems to function adequately. I hope that French speaking immigrants who otherwise would not be admissible to this country will not enter Switzerland for the purpose of using Switzerland as the road that leads to this country.
I know that as strong a federalist as the minister will not wish to see two immigration departments in the country. I hope we will not see two departments and I hope we will not play the numbers game to which I have referred. At this point I might ask, what is the goal for next year? Are we to do better in this regard than last year? Personally I think it would be better not to count separately the numbers of English speaking and French speaking immigrants entering the country. This aspect of immigration might be
October 26, 1967

Supply-Manpower and Immigration left unmeasured. I think all immigrants ought to be made equally welcome to this country.
Finally I wish to raise a question about a subject that has been brought to my attention. The hon. member for Greenwood spoke about refugees and their problem. Is the government working on a project to bring to Canada some of the Tibetan refugees who fled from their country when it was overrun by communist China and who entered India, a country that is sorely burdened with overpopulation. I have seen some of these people in the Himalayan region of India where their prospects are extremely limited because the country is overpopulated. At the present time we are taking from India a fairly sizeable number of immigrants who, because of their educational and technical qualifications, are needed in this country. These people are playing a very important role in our development. It might be one way of aiding India in a rather unusual and different direction if instead of simply taking the cream, the best people their educational system offers, we endeavoured to alleviate in some small way their refugee problem.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, most members of the house welcome the helpful and reasoned statement presented today by the minister and his assurance that as soon as possible a new immigration act will be considered and introduced in the house. I am sure the minister will consider all reasonable suggestions made by members of the committee. Those who know the minister and have had experience in dealing with him know that he is a man of strong views but that when reasonable suggestions are made he considers and adopts them.
The hon. member for Greenwood referred to section 61 of the Immigration Act which does permit the making of discrimatory regulations. In the past discriminatory regulations have been made under this section. However, the new regulations introduced by the minister and effective October 1 completely removed all vestiges of discrimination under the law and regulations as they now exist. The hon. member for Greenwood also referred to the section of the Immigration Act relating to prohibited persons. This is another section which, when the new act is introduced, must be considered very carefully and the necessary reforms made.
As the hon. member for Greenwood knows, under the present statute the minister has
[Mr. Johnston.l
wide discretion to issue ministerial permits to allow the entry of persons who may fall within the prohibited classes. I believe that this discretion has been exercised by the minister in a very fair and reasonable manner. Nevertheless, it is desirable that as soon as possible a new immigration act should be introduced. Hon. members in the committee today realize the volume of legislation before the house. Perhaps, as one unkind observer has implied, we in this house suffer from legislative constipation and need a procedural enema. In the meantime, however, a great deal can be done under the existing legislation by means of enlightened regulations and an enlightened administration of the law and the regulations. I suggest to members of the committee that we have been getting this from the present Minister of Manpower and Immigration.
Hear, hear.

I would particularly like to draw the attention of the committee to the very encouraging increase in the number of immigrants who have come to Canada in recent years. The figures I have indicate that in 1961 the number of immigrants admitted to Canada was 71,689. In 1962 the number was 74,586. In 1963, the first year under the present Liberal government, the number was 93,151. In 1964 the number was 112,606. In
1965	the number increased to 146,758. In
1966	the number increased still further to 194,743. In the period from January 1 to August 31 this year the number increased even more, by 27 per cent, and amounted to 125,836 for that part of the year. It is quite clear that this year substantially more than 200,000 immigrants will come to this country and make their homes here.
I hope the hon. member for Ontario is taking note of these figures.

These figures indicate that the rate of immigration at the present time is three times higher than it was in 1961 when a Conservative government was in power. The low figure for 1961 may not have been due to any lack of will on the part of the then Conservative government but may rather have resulted from the massive unemployment which then existed and which the government then in office appeared to be unable to do anything about.

Or a mixture of both.
October 26. 1867	COMMONS

Possibly a mixture of both. I find it difficult to overemphasize the importance and the value to Canada of this large inflow of immigrants. The whole question of immigration was very carefully considered several years ago by a commission of the United Church which studied immigration and its effects on Canada. The commission published a report which contains some very interesting and useful information even though it is now several years out of date. For example, it pointed out that statistics of post-war immigration show that three quarters of the immigrants coming to Canada are adults, one-half are workers and most of the workers are young people in the most productive age group between 20 and 44. For example, the report says that of the 124,700 immigrants who arrived in Canada in 1958 more than 58,000 were between the ages of 15 and 29. Canadian surveys of immigration figures for other years also emphasize the youthful character of immigrants. Not only were they workers, they were young workers and, more important, they have been skilled workers.
A Department of Labour report indicates that about two thirds of the net addition of professional engineers and draftsmen since the end of world war II have been immigrants. Another Department of Labour survey shows that 35 per cent of the skilled and highly skilled trade positions in Canadian industries in 1956 were occupied by immigrants who had received their trades training abroad. These youthful, skilled workers have performed an invaluable function upon which our present prosperity has been largely based.
Not only have these immigrants brought new skills to Canada but they have also brought a substantial amount of new capital. The report by the commission of the United Church points out that between 1946 and 1962 immigrants brought to Canada over $1 billion in capital and almost half a billion dollars worth of settlers' effects. They have established numerous new businesses in Canada which have provided employment for Canadians. The report points out that from 1950 to 1962, 9,850 new Canadians established businesses of their own for which they paid over $116 million. Of this sum they made cash payments in excess of $72 million. These new businesses created employment for almost 45,000 Canadians.
In 1961 the research staff of the department of citizenship and immigration made a survey of 7,000 immigrants who had obtained .heir Canadian citizenship papers. Of this
DEBATES	3521
Supply-Manpower and Immigration group about 350 had established their own businesses and created jobs for over 3,400 other Canadians. In other words, these 350 newcomers created new jobs equal to almost half of the entire group of immigrants under survey.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
It is apparent therefore that immigrants who seek entry to Canada do not seek entry as supplicants and should not be treated as such. They should be welcomed as guests who are bringing valuable gifts to this country. I believe I saw figures which indicate that almost half of the total number of immigrants to Canada have come to the Toronto area. Certainly Toronto has good reason to rejoice in the number of immigrants who have come to our city. It is upon their efforts and with their help that the post-war growth and prosperity of our citizens have been founded.
Because of the importance of the department, and indeed I can think of few other departments of the government which are of equal importance, it is absolutely essential that the facilities and service provided by the department should be first rate. I wish to congratulate the minister upon the improvement which he has made in the facilities, the staff and the services provided by the department. Many years ago some of us had the impression that the old department of citizenship and immigration was to some extent an orphan, cramped and restricted by its budget and perhaps not given the same consideration as certain more glamourous-appearing departments. The minister has done a great deal to upgrade its status and to improve the facilities and the service provided by the department not only abroad but in Canada. The importance of the department certainly justifies these efforts.
While I am on my feet perhaps I might refer to two difficult problems. I am sure that the success which has met the minister's efforts to date indicates that he will be able to resolve these problems successfully. In the manpower service, which is so essential to our national well-being, I suggest that we should consider very carefully and avoid duplication of any service now being provided in a satisfactory manner by private agencies. I say this not because I think that private industry should have a monopoly in any field of labour placement but simply because the revenues and expenditures of any governmental department are limited
3522	COMMONS
Supply-Manpower and Immigration and therefore must be spent in the best and most effective manner.
If in fact placement services are being satisfactorily provided by private agencies, then there would seem to be little purpose in incurring public expense and duplicating such facilities. I know, for example that there are many efficient private agencies in the larger centres which specialize in filling vacancies for skilled and white collar employees. If these agencies are in fact doing a good job, I hope the minister will not endeavour to duplicate them at the expense of the ordinary taxpayer.
The second problem, and one which has been referred to by a number of hon. members, relates to the necessity of preventing any gap developing between the federal and provincial programs involving retraining and vocational training. This matter has been referred to by most hon. members including the hon. members for Ontario, Greenwood, Roberval and Okanagan-Revelstoke, and clearly it is of vital importance and concern to most members of the committee. It is a difficult problem because, as all members of the committee know, it involves the most delicate relations between the federal and the provincial governments. It involves coordinating the federal responsibility for maintaining full employment with the provincial responsibility for education and social services.
The hon. member for Greenwood in particular referred to the fact that school drop-outs and hippies were not able to benefit from the present federal program. I believe the minister is aware of the necessity to co-ordinate very carefully the federal program for retraining those who have been thrown out of employment as a result of technological change with the provincial programs and the provincial responsibility in the fields of education and social service. It is a very delicate and difficult problem and one which does not admit of any easy solution. It is a question to which the minister will have to devote himself, and I am sure he will work closely with the provincial authorities in solving it successfully.
In the same general field there is of course another important principle to observe. The minister must be very careful that federal moneys which are administered by provincial authorities are well spent. This is the responsibility of the federal government. If federal moneys are provided we must make certain that the provincial government is spending

DEBATES	October 26, 1967
them properly and with the best possible effect.
Suggestions have been made that some of the training programs in the province of Ontario which are administered by provincial agencies are not administered with maximum efficiency. Again this involves very delicate and difficult problems of co-operation between the federal and provincial departments. Sometimes it appears to me that it is very difficult to get proper co-ordination and co-operation at the departmental level between provincial and federal authorities and I have often thought it would be desirable for the minister or for federal ministers in general to experiment with the creation of joint federal-provincial agencies with perhaps community involvement to avoid this particular problem. I believe that the minister's department may perhaps be experimenting with agencies along that line.
There is one extremely important reform for which the minister deserves a great deal of credit and a great deal of support from all members of the house. Under the regulations which became effective at the beginning of this month the principle of racial equality has been finally and completely established in our immigration laws. I believe it was the hon. member for Roberval who referred to the continuing discrimination under the citizenship laws or regulations. If I am correct in my belief, these are not administered by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration but by the Secretary of State, so I will not discuss them at this time. Under our present immigration regulations and laws, certainly the last vestiges of racial discrimination have been removed. I believe that they have been removed in practice as well. Sometimes practice is more important than the letter of the law.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
To illustrate the fact that discrimination has been reduced in practice over recent years I should like to refer to the figures on Chinese immigration. In 1961, Mr. Chairman, the number of Chinese admitted to Canada totalled 894. In 1962 the number went down to 876. In 1963, the first year of the Liberal government, the number almost doubled to 1,571. In 1964 the number doubled again to 3,210. In 1965 the number increased to 5,234. In 1966 the number was slightly lower, 5,178. From January 1 to June 30 of this year, the number admitted was 3,173 an increase of 32 per cent over the corresponding period in the previous year.
October 26, 1967	COMMONS
It is apparent, therefore, that at the present time, the rate of immigration to Canada in so far as Chinese are concerned is over seven times as high as it was in 1961 under a Conservative administration. I am particularly interested in these figures because many members of the Chinese community live in my riding of St. Paul's in Toronto. I thought that members of the committee might be interested in these figures as an illustration of what has been done in practice to overcome the racial discrimination which in previous years disgraced the administration of our immigration laws.
I think I should mention also, as an example of what is actually being done in practice, that the present application form for landed immigrants which became effective October 1 deletes any reference to the country of ethnic origin. I believe this is indicative of the intent of the minister in these regulations. Perhaps more important in so far as practice is concerned is the fact that for the first time the factors which should be taken into account by immigration officials who actually assess the intended immigrants are set out very clearly.
The hon. member for Greenwood expressed some apprehension about what he called the points system. He mentioned that in the interview with a proposed immigrant the immigration official is required to make a personal assessment of the character of the immigrant and to take into account such factors as adaptability, motivation, initiative and similar qualities. The hon. member for Greenwood expressed some apprehension as to what might happen if some immigration official had the opportunity of making a personal character assessment of him. I will make no comment one way or the other with regard to his fear. I believe it is unfounded. Instead I simply point out the hon. member for Greenwood that every day each of us is required to make an assessment of the character of people, and immigration officials are no different from the rest of us. In practice I assume they will act fairly. Despite the complaints which are inevitable in a department such as this, the general record of the department has been good.
This completes the remarks I should like to make at this point, Mr. Chairman. In closing I would simply say that I am particularly impressed by the fairness of the regulations which have been introduced by the minister.
I welcome those provisions which widen the classes of relatives that can be admitted to Canada, either on a sponsored or nominated 27053-223

Supply-Manpower and Immigration basis. This will mean that a great many more families will be reunited, and this is of great social importance. I welcome the new appeal procedure which has been introduced. This is the first time we have had a meaningful appeal procedure in our immigration regulations. The new appeal procedure may be some indication of a move toward a principle which would be of great international importance, namely, that those of us who have had the good fortune to be born in this country cannot expect to monopolize a great country such as Canada. Perhaps those born in other countries who can qualify and who would make good citizens have a right to be admitted which should not be entirely dependent upon the uncontrolled discretion of those of us who happen to live here at the present time.

If I am speaking 6th, I will not prevent any member of the Progressive Conservative party or any other from speaking. If, anyway, there are 26 speakers, whether I speak 5th, 6th or 25th, they will be speaking more often than I, which I admit because they are more numerous.

rules. All of us want to get on with the business and to see it done, but one of the great weaknesses in the guillotine method of closing off debate on estimates is that serious questions put to a minister are sometimes never answered. For example, the other day I asked some ten questions of the Minister of Trade and Commerce about the grain problem, which is very important to the farmers of western Canada. The minister sat throughout the debate until the end of the day. Perhaps his estimates will not come before the committee again and I will never get an answer.
The hon. member for Ontario, a former minister of labour who conceived the vocational training program, part of which has been adopted by the government and part forgotten, asked some serious questions based on his experience as minister and on the fact that he is the chief critic on this subject for our party. However, it seems to be somewhat an exercise in futility if we put questions to ministers and never get answers. After all, the idea of debating estimates is not just to make a pretty little speech but to find out ministers' programs.
By way of introduction to this point, Mr. Chairman, this might be a good time to read words which have been quoted with approval by the present Prime Minister, words approved by the former prime minister who sits in this house, words used by Arthur Meighen. Under the procedure which prevailed in the old days we could say to a minister that his estimates were not going to go through until he gave us some answers. I am not referring to this minister personally; I just give that as an example. But now we ask questions which are just left in Hansard and are never answered. How can the members of the opposition do their work if that is the way we in this house have to operate?
May I ask the members of the committee why they believe I am not going to give any answers?

I hope the minister will, but other ministers have not. I believe that this minister is very congenial and is liked by members on both sides of the house. I can see he is the sort who would be liked outside the house as well, not only in his constituency but in any part of the country, because he is that type of man. But with the greatest respect to him, we have not had from other ministers answers to questions we have put on Hansard.

I should like to tell the committee what Arthur Meighen said. I am not going to read the whole speech but these words were quoted with approval by the present Prime Minister when speaking to one of the clubs in Ottawa. I think they have also been quoted with approval in this house by the former prime minister who sits on this side. Arthur Meighen said:
It should supervise all expenditures and prevent overexpenditure by exposing to the light of public opinion wasteful expenditures or worse. It finds fault; it suggests amendments; it asks questions and elicits information-
We have been asking questions and trying to elicit information but have been unsuccessful.
-it arouses, educates and moulds public opinion by voice and vote. It must scrutinize every action by the government and in doing so prevents the shortcuts through democratic procedure that governments like to make.
The absence of a strong opposition means a one-party state. A one-party state means an all-powerful cabinet.
That is what we have today, Mr. Chairman, an all-powerful cabinet. Perhaps these new rules will be made permanent or they may be changed. But if the new rules mean that questions we ask members of the government are never going to be answered, then they are being used as a guillotine to keep government information in the drawers so it cannot be made public.
The government's expenditures this year are the highest of any government. That has been pointed out over and over again. Compared with the expenditures of the United States government the expenditures of this government have risen 25 per cent, and the United States is fighting a war. The opposition cannot get information about the expenditure of millions and millions of dollars on the part of hon. gentlemen on the front benches opposite. Those, Mr. Chairman, are my words of introduction to the minister and I want other ministers to read them and think about this point. These new rules must not be allowed to prevent us getting the kind of information we require.
To show how important this point is I should like to use this illustration. I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether he spoke to the United States government about dumping approximately 100 million bushels of wheat in our eastern markets, and I have not had an answer. I also asked him whether there would ever be a dollar subsidy paid, because we will never sell wheat below the floor price set by the agreement, and that 27053-2231

Mr. Chairman, I was talking about my position in connection with the rules. I shall leave that subject now. I have always felt that it is a proper thing to amalgamate or correlate departments of government if greater efficiency is likely to result, so when I heard there was to be a department of manpower which would be able to supervise immigration policies, pools of labour, vocational training and so on, I thought it was a good idea. But the new department will be effective only to the extent that the minister receives co-operation from his fellow ministers. He cannot be successful alone.
My hon. friend from Ontario drew attention to some of the weaknesses of the program which has been put forward. I doubt

that the minister will ever be able to implement this program effectively, nor do I believe he will be able to make the changes suggested by my hon. friend. He cannot do so because he will not receive co-operation from the Minister of Finance. That is his problem.
I am one of those who believe we are facing in this country a serious financial situation brought on by the present government. As a result the Minister of Manpower and Immigration will have to bear a lot more responsibility in the near future than he has done up to now. Lay-offs are taking place and we are moving into a future when they will be more frequent. I want to come to grips with one situation of which I have personal knowledge.
On Thursday night and on Friday I was absent from this house. We hear a lot about absenteeism. Where was I? I had been invited to speak to a meeting in Calgary arranged because 400 men had been laid off by the C.P.R. You cannot just sit here in Ottawa if you want to know what is going on. You have to move around.
Briefly, there are between 800 and 1,000 men employed in the workshops at a place called Ogden in tho suburbs of Calgary. These workshops have been there for years employing highly skilled people. The payroll is large. What has happened? The labour union cannot get answers from the C.P.R. One morning 400 men were laid off. The company said it was only for a month, possibly for two months. But the men are not sure. I asked the minister to tell us what the situation there is. He was most courteous. He told the house today that those 400 men, or some of them at least, were already back on the job. This was the information available to him through the department. I have checked with the union and they tell me that this is not correct, that in fact there are still 400 men working out of the 800 but that the 400 who were laid off are still without work.
I know the minister would not come into the house and misrepresent the facts as he knew them in any way. He gave us the facts as they were made known to him. He said that many of the men were back, more than half; I have not checked the blues-

On this point, perhaps I did not express myself clearly. I said they had been called back to work. This does not mean they are actually back at their jobs.
October 26, 1967	COMMONS

Well, when I hear "called back to work" I assume it applies to tomorrow morning, not to next year. I am told they have been laid off for a month or two months. This matter is within the minister's sphere of responsibility. I believe there is a scheme on foot to move these workshops out of Calgary. What will happen to these men in such an eventuality? Most of them are over 45; some are in their fifties and some are in their sixties. It is all very well for the minister to say they will be able to move elsewhere and find alternative employment. We all know how difficult it is for men over 45 to find work; they cannot, as a rule, find alternative employment today.
We are all familiar with what happened in Winnipeg. We know what happened when Air Canada moved its shops. I believe the same process is going on under the C.P.R. I have been informed that the company is now contracting the repair of its big diesels with General Motors. This is a foot in the door to get rid of its own facilities. Why have these men been laid off? I am talking about correlation and I intend to correlate my speech today. I will tell you why, Mr. Chairman. It is because the Minister of Trade and Commerce has not come clean in this house on the subject of wheat.
The men to whom I have referred are employed repairing cars which are used to haul wheat to Vancouver and the great lakes. Today there is no wheat movement; cars are piled up all over western Canada. Wheat is not moving from the farms and the call for cars has declined accordingly. The Globe and Mail says the farmers are being subsidized. I say the editor should go to western Canada. He would not have to worry about a single dollar finding its way into the pockets of the farmers, because no wheat is being sold. Some tremendous speeches were made on this subject the other night by hon. members from western Canada. It may be that the C.P.R. will use this situation as an excuse for closing down its shops and farming out the repair work to General Motors.
Let me tell the minister that when 1,000 men are thrown out of work in a city with a population of 250,000 it really makes an impact. In the area of Ogden itself it is a matter of economic life or death. Our problem does not affect the Department of Manpower and Immigration alone. The hon. gentleman is, I believe, one of the leaders of his party in Quebec. He is either the leader or the second in command of the Liberal party there. It is a great thing to gather a lot of
DEBATES	3527
Supply-Manpower and Immigration responsibilities under one roof, but the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce will not come clean. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, for whom I have a lot of affection personally, went to the United States and said: "What are you doing, breaking your word to 52 nations by shipping wheat at lower prices and taking away the export markets of Canada and other countries?" I asked questions day in and day out on this point when the former minister of transport was here and was ruled out of order. That was the great parliamentarian Jack Pickersgill who was able to leave the house and get a job for himself at $40,000 a year. I warned him about another problem. Let me read this to the minister. The hon. gentleman is not to be blamed for it; I am his defence counsel this evening. He is trying to do his job but he is carrying a load placed upon him by these other fellows. Just listen to this from the Financial Post:
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
The U.S. has won long-term coal agreements from Japan for shipment of coking coal for metallurgical use in the face of competition from Canada, Australia-
Key factor in the United States deal-
What was the key factor? I say to the minister that his colleagues in the government sit around and do nothing.
-it may run to $1,500,000,000 over the next ten years-is the shipping cost which has been "bugging" Alberta-B.C. coal mine operators. Japan has received assurances of stability in freight rates-
It has received those assurances from the United States. What has the C.P.R. done with this contract? I asked Mr. Pickersgill over and over again when he was the minister of transport. He replied that the C.P.R. was a private corporation and he did not want to interfere with it. Now he is gone, having landed himself a big hot-shot job for $40,000 a year. If any Tory had introduced a bill to create a job for himself worth $40,000 a year there would have been headlines about it in every newspaper. Mr. Chairman, we are dealing with the estimates of a department that is as important as any in the federal government today. Manpower and immigration policies are crucial to the continued successful existence and development of this country.
The hon. member who just spoke has treated us to one of his usual colourful displays. Read the Gallup poll. The memory of the Canadian people is not short so far as the Liberal party is concerned.

We shall see when the time comes. Polls come and go. Though members of the official opposition have themselves commented about this sort of thing, as well in the past. One of the two halves of the department deals with manpower. Certainly this department, and particularly this section, has a key role in improving the productivity of this country. It is not enough merely to build buildings in the way that was done by the party of the Acting Leader of the Opposition and to fill them with people who in many cases were trained for jobs that did not exist. This government has recognized the need not only to see that buildings are built and classrooms are filled but also that workers are matched to skills, that real information is available as to the skills required in this country, and that training of all sorts is encouraged in ways that mean that people who want to do so will be financially able to take courses that are offered across this country.
This is the type of necessary work that is being carried out by this new department as its reorganization proceeds. There are facilities that did not exist before this department came into existence in its present form, facilities to determine the jobs required in this country, to determine the skills required, to match people to jobs, to make sure that we have not only the necessary courses available but that courses match the requirements of this country for the skills of today and the future.
Let us look at some examples. Let us look at the separation of the national employment service from the unemployment insurance commission, the turning of it into an active

agency of manpower policy and its transformation, going on at this time, into the Canada manpower centres. This move was undertaken by this government and the minister's department under the leadership of the minister, a move that has been greeted with praise and encouragement by thoughtful observers across the country.

I should like at this time, Mr. Chairman, to turn to the other side of the minister's department, namely, the immigration branch. Certainly the new regulations for the selection of immigrants, the new points system, is a step forward in the creation of methods for the fair, reasonable and humane selection of people to join with us in building this country.
These regulations broaden the classes of relatives who can be considered. They are aimed at treating people on an equal basis no matter where they come from in this world. The points system provides a flexibility that was not present under the former rigid approach whereby a person either qualified completely on the basis of skill or fell within a narrow category with regard to relatives who could sponsor him, and if he did not fall completely in one area or the other he could not come to this country.
At the present time, under this new system, if a person does not have a very high level of education, complete training in a skill, but there are other factors that can be taken into account, relatives willing to support him, a certain knowledge of our two official languages, these things can be added together in a way that should make it possible for the person who wants to come to this country and contribute to its development to come here and make a better life for himself and his family, to the benefit of all of us.
But while I am praising these new regulations and praising the minister for responding to the suggestions of the immigration committee, of members on this side of the house and the other side who helped bring about this new system, I should say that I do not think the present structure of the points system should be regarded as being engraved on tablets of stone.
A certain period must go by in which the administration of the points system as constituted at the present time should be studied and observed. But I think it would be a great

Supply-Manpower and Immigration mistake if after a period of study and transition, which should not be too long, the government failed to take into account the actual experience of administering this system and treated the points system as something immutable, as something handed down from above that cannot be changed without threatening the very structure and foundation of this country. This would be a mistake.
Although the program has been in operation for a relatively brief period, we can see some areas of it, some aspects, which I think give cause for concern. I refer particularly to the section of the regulations entitled "Norms For Assessment of Independent Applicants" and in particular to the category "Personal assessment" which reads as follows:
Adaptability, motivation, initiative, resourcefulness and other similar qualities to be assessed during an interview with the applicant by an immigration or visa officer, the total assessment up to a maximum of 15 to reflect the latter's judgment of the personal suitability of the applicant and his family to become successfully established in Canada.
The minister may well say: The reason we provide this category and assign it 15 points is to help people to come into this country when they may not be able to measure up completely to the other norms of education and training, occupational demand, occupational skill, age, and so on.
I certainly agree with that, but I am somewhat concerned that this particular category can be used in exactly the opposite way. Let me explain why I say this. First of all, 15 points are given for personal assessment. This is almost the same number of points as for education and training, which category provides up to a maximum of 20 points. It is exactly the same number of points as for occupational demand, which provides a maximum of 15 points. It is more than the number of points for occupational skill, for which a total of ten points is provided. It is certainly more than the number of points provided where the applicant has a relative who is not eligible to sponsor him but is willing to assist to some extent. Only five points are given here.
I suggest that as we obtain further experience in administering this points system we may find that too many points have been given to the category of personal assessment. At least the other categories are capable of some degree of objective measurement and objective definition. But this clearly cannot be done with this category of personal assessment, where the officer has to consider such

DEBATES	October 26. 1967
qualities as adaptability, motivation, initiative, resourcefulness, and so on. These are all wonderful words and are qualities we look for in immigrants, but I have some doubt whether any one of them can be assessed by an immigration officer in the course of an interview of 15 or 20 minutes.
These terms have been the subject of consideration and study by social scientists and researchers in universities for many years. I have grave doubts whether even they can provide, even after a period of lengthy research and study, definitions and criteria which can be established and applied to people in a way which permits decisions to be made on the crucial question of whether people being tested have the qualifications to come into this country.
Shortly before the time came when I would be able to speak on these estimates I went into the parliamentary library and found a volume entitled "A Dictionary of the Social Sciences" which was compiled under the auspices of the United Nations educational, scientific, and cultural organization. The book is described as containing terms pertinent to the fields of anthropology, economics, political science, social psychology and sociology. It occurred to me that if the minister has teams of sociologists studying the reasons why immigrants are not interested in coming to this country from certain other countries- and I think this is a very useful work-possibly similar efforts would have been aimed at evolving the category of personal assessment. Therefore I decided to look up the terms in this dictionary. First I looked up the term "adaptability". The term "adaptability" does not even occur in this book; it is not there at all. Since I do not want to be unfair, I would point out that the word "adaptation" does appear, and it is defined as follows on page 8:

Adaptation may be defined as the process, and the resultant condition, in which changes in an organism, system of social organization, group, or culture aid the survival, functioning, maintenance, or achievement of purpose on the part of an organism, personality, group, culture, or any part thereof.
I wonder if an immigration officer can apply this definition to an individual after an interview of 15 minutes or of several hours, because subparagraph 1 of this definition reads as follows:
As can be seen the present usage of the term has become so broad as to be diffuse and almost meaningless.

Then I decided to turn to the next term which is "motivation" for which there is a rather lengthy definition in the book, part of which I will read:
The term motivation refers to any organismic state that mobilizes activity which is in some sense selective, or directive, with respect to the environment. Since a great deal of human behaviour that is obviously motivated, in this sense, cannot be directly associated with any specific, discriminable organismic states, it is necessary to distinguish one motive from another in terms of the goals (q.v.) toward which behaviour is directed, if the term is to have a constant meaning regardless of whether or not the motive in question corresponds to a specific, known physiologic state.
I know the minister shares with me the aim to have our system administered in a fair and equitable way, and he has achieved remarkable progress along these lines. Perhaps he could tell me what training has been given to our immigration officers to assist them to apply the criteria in this definition to an individual in 10 or 15 minutes.
The next term is "initiative". I looked it up and found its definition to be as follows:
The initiative is a political device-used widely in Switzerland and in state and local governments in the United States-through which the electorate may by petition propose a statute or an amendment to a constitution.
It goes on to define this concept at greater length. I think it is of some significance that the term "initiative" does not even exist as a concept in social sciences applicable to the individual human personality, and yet the department is asking its officers to assess applicants who wish to live in this country on the basis of a concept of initiative which hundreds of social scientists at the level of people like Clyde Kluckhorn, Margaret Mead and Barbara Ward have not been able to define in this volume published under the aegis of UNESCO.
Then I turn to another term, namely "resourcefulness" and this is not in the book either. What I just said about initiative obviously also applies to the term "resourcefulness".

remarks. Since I will try not to speak at great length, there should be some time left for questions.

I want to deal with another point which has less reference to the points system as such than to the present method of considering the applications of visitors. I understand that a person who applies for an immigration
October 26, 1967

Supply-Manpower and Immigration visa while visiting this country is not given any credit for arranged employment in Canada but automatically loses 10 points. It seems to me that if we are really interested in encouraging skilled people to come here we should welcome those who come here on a trip of an exploratory nature to see whether they can fit into our society. It is unrealistic to expect someone who has a home and a good job to give it all up and to come to this country, even after having had the opportunity to read all the leaflets and talk to the immigration officers in his home country, without having a chance to study the situation personally. I certainly think it should be possible for someone to come here as a visitor to see whether or not he likes the country and can find a suitable job, and then file his application in a way which would not discriminate against him. His application should certainly not be considered more quickly than it would be if he were to remain in his home country and file it there, but I do not think he should start out with a couple of strikes against him because he came here to visit and decided he wanted to stay. It is unreasonable to expect such a person to incur the expenses involved in buying a ticket to go back home an amount which may be sufficient for him to pay to bring his family over, and then have to make an application back in his home country.
When the minister will speak later on in the debate perhaps he may provide some clarification with regard to the deduction of points where arranged employment is made. I think it would be most unreasonable if this deduction were to take place after the prospective immigrant came here and arranged for employment, especially if in the first place he did not intend to stay here permanently but, at the urging of relatives decided to apply and told the immigration officer that he has found someone who wanted to offer him a job in his trade. If we can accept the argument of the department that there is something wrong in having a more open acceptance of applications from visitors, one should also possibly be able to accept the argument that some points should be deducted if a person comes here after making prior arrangements for a job here and arrives here ostensibly as a visitor. Certainly this argument cannot be applied to a person who comes here as a visitor and, at the urging of a prospective employer, comes to the immigration officer and says he would like to stay here. I think it is unreasonable, under those circumstances to take ten points from the

points available to him. I urge the minister to give further consideration to this aspect as well.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman. I will say that while I have attempted to put forward some criticisms in a constructive vein of some aspects of this points system, I feel it is a great step forward, a great improvement over the previous approach to the selection of immigrants. My remarks are aimed at helping the system work better, at helping the minister achieve continued and even greater success in his responsibility, not only in this department but as one of the leaders of the government of this country. After all, in spite of the criticism that may come from this side of the house, or the other side, I think the memories of the people of this country are not so short that they cannot remember that in the early 1960's when the party now in opposition formed the government, immigration fell to some 70,000.
It was only after this government took office that the number of immigrants rose in a way which reflected the needs of the country, and a better approach to the humane treatment of our fellow human beings. Certainly, there is a great difference, no matter what criticisms I or others may bring forward during the study of these estimates, between the almost 200,000 immigrants who have come this year and the 70,000 who came under the former government. This shamefully low figure along with others was a blot on the record of that government.
So, in conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I say that I have put forward some suggestions for improvement. I commend the minister upon his willingness to listen to suggestions and to consider individual cases as well. I am confident that the department, under his leadership and the government of which he is a member, will continue the progress that came about only when this government took office, and will continue to provide the necessary increase in immigrants for the benefit of this country and its people.
Mr. Chairman, after listening to the previous speaker-

I have a question which I should like to direct to the hon. member for Essex West. The hon. member was critical of certain concepts involved in the new immigration policy. In particular, he stated that the use of certain terms, such as initiative,

were difficult to express because they lacked precision. I should like to ask him if he would agree that we have the same problem when this term is used in connection with economics and taxation. This term is used so frequently, that I ask him if he would not agree there is an equal lack of justification for its use?

No, I would not accept that statement. There are dictionary definitions, but I think there is a difference between dictionary definitions and the more precise definition required when one operates in the area of the sciences, even the social sciences. I will be the first to agree that the social sciences have not yet achieved the absolute certainty that some of the other sciences have. While I believe that my criticisms are valid in respect of the attempt to use the word "initiative" as a concept in the measurement of individual human performance or potential performance, I think that as a broad general concept related to the activities of people, parties, governments or humanity in general it is capable of continued use. Certainly it has justification in so far as the achievements of this government to date are concerned.

Interesting, indeed, Mr. Chairman, has been the speech of the hon. member for Essex West. He has sought to set himself up as one of the principal critics of the department of immigration, and yet when the chips are down he wants to go along with and be part of the minister's policy. Really, he cannot have it both ways. He puts one foot firmly on each side of the fence, while the wire eats into his soul. This is the type of operation of which the hon. gentleman has been guilty in the joint special committee. In the committee he has set himself up as someone trying to be in opposition to the department, and yet he comes into the house and takes an entirely different approach. Sir, I do not believe I can make any other comment except, "Oh, consistency, thou art a jewel."
He is having a love-in this afternoon.
May I ask a question?
I listened with care to the hon. gentleman and I hope he will listen with equal care to me.

During the last session of parliament immigration policy was considered in detail in a joint special committee of the Senate and House of Commons. In my view this was a good committee. It is regrettable that the government and its supporters have not seen fit to continue the work of that committee at this session, so that a proper report could be made to parliament and acted upon.
The committee itself was established on May 18, and the members of the committee were appointed on May 29. There has not been one sitting of the committee since May 29. The responsibility rests with the government whip to call that committee. No one else but the government whip can call it. This is neglect of a very vital issue on the part of the government whip.
The briefs that were submitted to the joint special committee at the last session were of an exceptionally high calibre. They deserved, but have not received, the intensive study of the members of the committee. The house, and I think the nation, are entitled to a detailed and exhaustive study of the provisions of the white paper.
In earlier debates, sir, I have expressed my opinion that the white paper was window dressing. It needs to be strengthened greatly and clarified before it could become an acceptable basis for a long range, genuinely expansionist immigration policy. The evidence taken before the special committee clearly indicates that while the white paper purports to be expansionist it is, in fact, latently restrictive; that while purportedly non-discriminatory it is latently discriminatory.

Mr. Chairman, just before the recess I had endeavoured to deal with the inconsistencies of the white paper, equalled only by the jewelled inconsistencies of the hon. member for Essex West. I should like to continue and to deal with some of the briefs which have been submitted on behalf of a variety of organizations and governments to the special joint committee on immigration.
I thought the most impressive brief of all was that submitted by the government of Manitoba. The minister of industry and commerce, Hon. Sidney Spivak, pointed out that each economic region of Canada has special problems related to the need for immigrants, each its own particular potentials, problems and objectives.
While it is certainly true that the more heavily developed and industrialized regions of Canada may require more skilled and fewer unskilled immigrants, the less developed areas of Canada actually require more unskilled and semi-skilled immigrants. I think a brief quotation from the Manitoba brief, as it appears at page 199 of the proceedings and evidence of the special joint committee, will make this particular point:
The policy proposed in the white paper claims to be nondiscriminatory. It is in terms of geography and race. But it does in fact discriminate against the kind of people Manitoba needs today to enable our economy to expand and grow. The federal "policy" is not expansionist as it claims. Rather it imposes unrealistic standards in a small and highly selective, increasingly competitive skill and education market. It simply does not recognize the facts.
That is the point I should like to make about the white paper, Mr. Chairman: It simply does not recognize the facts. It does not seem to me that the new regulations adopting a points system are adequate enough or flexible enough to meet this point of view. In many ways I would prefer what I

DEBATES	October 26, 1967
have heard described as the old "eyeball" system.
The hon. gentleman from Greenwood was worried that he might not be admitted to Canada if suddenly he were confronted by an immigration officer who, looking him over and applying the points system, sought to describe him. For myself, Mr. Chairman, I like the eyeball system. I believe in the judgment of the individual by the properly trained immigration officer.
I repeat, sir, what I have said before often in this chamber, that if the ancestors of the members of this chamber had had to meet the selection criteria laid down in the white paper, few of us would even be citizens of this country of which we are now representatives in the parliament of the nation.
I venture to put on record, Mr. Chairman, the recommendations of the Manitoba brief, and respectfully to endorse them in full, as they appear at page 200 of the proceedings and evidence of the special joint committee on immigration:
The following recommendations respecting Canada's immigration policies and programs are submitted for consideration:
National immigration policy is not sufficiently flexible to meet the needs of each region and province. Programs should be specifically designed to help overcome regional disparities.
Critical labour shortages cannot be met because of existing immigration rules. Procedures should be established immediately which will permit prompt immigration action to overcome existing and future persistent labour shortages.
Proposed immigration policy will hamper "frontier" development. Special programs should be created to help encourage "frontier" development-
Rigid admission standards based primarily on education are unrealistic and do not meet needs of the economy. They are discriminatory rather than expansionist. Education and skill admission standards should be revised to take account of the immigrant's aptitude and potential.
Those words I would adopt in full, Mr. Chairman. I say to the committee that nowhere has the failure of our immigration policy been so evident as in the recruitment of agricultural workers. The extent to which the department of immigration has let down the farmers of this nation is exposed in an answer to a question of mine which appears in Hansard for June 21, 1967 at page 1769. The third part of the question was:
3. Of the immigrants who were admitted to Canada in 1965 and 1966 (a) how many were destined for the agricultural labour force (b) what percentage of the total immigration inflow for each of the two years did these represent?
October 26, 1967	COMMONS
What was the answer, Mr. Chairman? In 1965 the workers destined for agricultural employment numbered 2,362; the percentage of the total immigration was 1.6. In 1966 the number was 3,153; the percentage of the total immigration was 1.6. In each of those years, Mr. Chairman, only 1.6 per cent of the total inflow of immigration was directed to agricultural employment, the industry which still today is the very bedrock of our national prosperity.
Yet every day, Mr. Chairman, more and more farmers are compelled to give up farming or to restrict their activities because of this shortage of labour; and no one knows that better than the man who with such distinction occupies the chair at the present time. The almost total lack of farm labour at this time is verging upon a national crisis as well as a personal tragedy for very many farmers. What plans has the department in this regard? None was outlined. Will the minister when he replies outline the plans the department has in this respect?
Another sufferer from the excessive emphasis upon skill and education is the mining industry. All of us have seen the recent press stories, which I am not going to read into the record, setting up the critical labour shortage in that industry. The department has been dilatory and negligent in its lack of recruitment programs for labour in these two basic industries.
[DOT] (8:10 p.ra.)
One of the major problems of the department results from the discrimination against the overseas staff which exists in comparison with the treatment accorded the overseas staff of the Department of External Affairs and the Department of Trade and Commerce. The officers of the department of immigration ought, as a matter of right, to enjoy the status and prestige accorded at least to the overseas staff of the Department of Trade and Commerce. They do not. Those men and women who are selecting our future citizens are engaged in work at least as important to Canada as those who are promoting our trade. The just grievances of the overseas staff of the department of immigration should be removed at once.
In his reply, I would ask the minister to tell the committee what action has been taken to promote the immigration of noncommunists from behind the iron curtain. We are told there are extensive pools of highly trained and intelligent people seeking to

Canadians of Polish origin are among our most enlightened and publicly minded citizens. The Canadian Polish Congress is a great national organization. This country could use many more citizens of the qualities of those of Polish origin.
Again, I should like the minister to tell us what co-operation has taken place between his department and the government of Manitoba in respect of the latter's program under which free passage is offered as a means of attracting immigrants to that province. Is this program a success? Ought it to be emulated on a national scale? Earlier, in the course of another debate, I expressed the view-which I reiterate now-that we should extend broader and more generous inducements with a view to attracting desirable immigrants. The Australian plan has worked; it has attracted to that great country a large number of most suitable immigrants who might otherwise have been admitted to Canada.
Turning to another subject, I submit with great respect that the minister has been less than vigilant, or less than expeditious, in getting the new immigration appeal board into full operation. There was an unconscionable delay in making the appointments, and the actual commencement of operations on a new basis was delayed much longer than we were led to expect. Why has this been the case? The board may well be the white hope in immigration policy. Let us give it every opportunity to build up a new and, I hope, humanitarian jurisprudence in the immigration field.
Mr. Chairman, a concomitant of the failure of the minister and the government to get the special committee into action is the further delay in the total revision of the obsolete, one might almost say antedeluvian, Immigration Act. The target date of the previous government for this revision was two years following the enactment of the new regulations in January, 1962. That target has been missed by 3| years. My advice to the minister is: Let us get on with this job. The Immigration Act is a hodge-podge of inconsistent antiquities. Let us bring it into the 20th century and make some attempt in its drafting to look forward to the 21st.

I believe the committee is entitled to a full statement from the minister about the progress of the department's program in connection with the granting of immigrant status for persons who overstay their visits to Canada, as outlined in the hon. gentleman's statement of July 8, 1966. At that time, there were certainly between 25,000 and 35,000 persons who were in Canada illegally. How many of these have since been legally admitted? How many new illegal entries have been made since that time, according to departmental estimates? Has the policy of July, 1966 solved this continuing problem, or has it merely settled some individual oases while ignoring the arrival of new illegal entrants?
Many members of this house have been concerned about the presence in Canada of so-called draft dodgers from the United States. The ease with which a United States citizen may enter Canada either as a visitor or as an immigrant is something no one wishes to restrict. I recognize equally that the whole of the North American continent, United States and Canada alike, owes a great deal to dissenters, religious, pacifist and otherwise. But I think this committee needs an assurance that we are not merely lending ourselves to the breach of the laws of our neighbour. We need to be assured, in the second place, that the admissions are legal, and that they are allowed for purposes which would serve our national interest. Third, we should be satisfied that the entrants are not persons of a type likely to engage in illegal or illicit activities while in Canada.
The minister owes the committee a detailed statement. I seek to place no impediment upon the proper and legal entry into Canada of United States citizens, including those who are genuine non-conformists, but I do not wish our country to be a haven for drug addicts, perverts and other escapists from reality.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, I have only a few words to say in this debate on the estimates of the Department of Manpower and Immigration. To begin with I would like to congratulate the minister. Since he came to Ottawa and was made minister in charge of this department he has been instrumental in introducing significant reforms both in immigration and manpower. The new rules for the admission of immigrants are a big step forward because they make a more realistic assessment of the true value of a potential immigrant. Previously too much value was given to the formal training of the immigrant and not enough to the other factors which make a person a good Canadian.
The new regulations have been directed to economic ends to correspond with our manpower needs. This is extremely important, but above this I believe the new rules with the points system are more humane, more just and more orderly. As a member of parliament from a city constituency which has a high percentage of immigrants, I have already found examples where the new rules have provided for a more humane and better flow of immigrants.
But with all new plans there are bound to be a few kinks which have to be worked out with experience. I merely want to mention a few of these and make some suggestions to the minister about them. I believe the most sensitive area in the new method and points system involves the men who interview prospective immigrants and apply the points system. One can easily see how easy it would be for the interviewer to let his personal prejudices influence his granting of points, especially in the areas where quick judgment is required, and where really no quick judgment can be made. It is to be hoped that all interviewers will be properly instructed, and I think they should be given more specific rules for guidance.
Supply-Manpower and Immigration
It appears to me, Mr. Chairman, that too often the interviewers and other officials in the department resolve any doubts against the prospective immigrant. It would seem to me that it would be much better and more humane to resolve any doubts in favour of the immigrant. Too often people have been refused entry or sent back to their own countries merely on what would appear to be the personal whim of the interviewer or of the official in the department. So, whereas I feel the new rules and regulations are a big step forward, and really the right sort of thing, it is most important that they be applied by people who would apply any doubt in favour of the applicant.
Although the new rules have removed any discrimination, they really will not be effective until we have placed more immigration officers and more personnel in countries where the demand for immigration is high, and where the pressures of the population explosions are also high. I have particularly in mind Indonesia, India, Hong Kong and the West Indies. I have encountered problems in my own constituency concerning prospective immigrants from these areas, involving people who have been waiting for years to get into Canada because of lack of personnel or lack of offices, many of them people with high qualifications and who, apparently, could become very good Canadians.
I realize that in the matter of immigrants coming from developing countries we must work in co-operation with those countries, so that we do not take away from them some of their own people who are needed to develop them. It would be ridiculous on the one hand for our government to try to assist the development of these countries through our external aid office and, on the other hand, take the people they need away from them.
I believe the minister has announced his intention of correcting other problems such as those concerned with the handicapped and mentally ill. The sooner amendments are made to the new rules, to allow an immigrant family to bring with them a member of that family who is chronically ill or handicapped, or who has some type of disease which would not permit his admission as an individual, provided the family is willing to take care of that person, the better it will be. It is completely inhumane to allow a family to come to Canada, yet disallow one brother or son merely because he has some type of illness which would bar his admission as an individual immigrant. So long as the family
3540	COMMONS
Supply-Manpower and Immigration is prepared to take care of him he should be allowed to come to Canada.
With regard to prospective immigrants from behind the Iron Curtain I have personally encountered problems where the security check involved takes too long and is applied with too much rigour against people who, in the long run, are often shown to have nothing against them which should prevent their coming into this country. I say we should allow such prospective immigrants to come into Canada provisionally, if they meet the test on all other points, with the stipulation that if anything shows up later in their security check then they would have to leave the country. I believe a somewhat similar procedure is followed in other countries.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I think the new policy we have introduced covering the manpower retraining program and the manpower relocation program is a big step forward in this age of technological change, in which men often lose their jobs in middle life because of new technology and new types of processing. However, I have found that some men who applied for the retaining program were refused admission because they were over the maximum age laid down. One man I have in mind was 56, and another 58.
I have also found instances of people who were refused because they did not have sufficient education under the regulations covering the retraining program. If this retraining program is to be really effective I believe it should apply to men who are in their middle age, even if they do not have grade 11 education. In one case I know that a man was refused because he did not have grade 11 education, and he wrote me about it. He was a man who had a trade, but who lost his job because of new technology. This man was refused retraining because he did not have grade 11 education. In other cases, as I have said, men were refused admission to a retraining program because it was claimed they were too old.
I believe that one of the most difficult areas in manpower is with respect to middle aged workers. Even if they can be retrained those of this age group have the most difficulty in finding jobs. I have found that many men of ability who still have much to offer Canada and to the economic growth of their regions cannot get jobs because of the restrictions many companies impose with respect to

age. The department responsible for manpower must work to correct this problem. We should do something to remedy restrictive rules in the department's regulations which prevent persons such as I have mentioned from entering into retraining and relocation programs because of age or education.
As I said at the beginning, the department's difficulties are kinks which will be ironed out. They are natural. I think the minister, in setting up this department and introducing into immigration and manpower new procedures, deserves a great deal of credit.

I shall try to be brief, for two reasons. First, many others wish to talk in this interesting debate and, second, the Leader of the Opposition in an able address covered many points I had wanted to cover. I shall not repeat them, except to urge on the minister the wisdom of letting a committee of the House of Commons examine this program and the work of this department. Probably that could be done next year. That way we could learn more than by having exchanges in the House of Commons. Experts could be called before the committee to testify. One point that could be looked into, for example, is the 25 per cent of unplaced job applicants registered with the former national employment service in 1966. They were male and over the age of 54. Only 1.2 per cent of those who were in training were in that age group. Obviously, those in the 54 and up age group face a serious problem. They may be regarded as untrainable for new jobs, or as not having the inclination at that time of life to take job training opportunities that are available.
On points such as these it would be useful to hear experts from inside and outside the department. The problem is a neglected one and perhaps cannot be solved by the Department of Manpower and Immigration. Nevertheless in a sense these people are being forgotten. I mention these matters to the minister in all earnestness, hoping that, say next year, a committee may be set up to examine in depth the operations of his department.
This afternoon, if I heard him correctly, the minister mentioned that the department was not concentrating its efforts in the area of moving people from one part of Canada to another. It preferred, and I hope I have this correctly, for problems to be solved in the provinces in which they occur. The President
October 26, 1967

of the Treasury Board who made a remark some years ago that brought a storm from Atlantic Canada about his ears will no doubt tell the minister that such an approach is wise.
Another aspect the committee could examine is the effectiveness over the last six years of the department's programs. In a powerful indictment published in the Monetary Times for June, 1967, an article entitled "The Manpower Mess", had this to say in part:
From 1961 to 1966 program 4 (training in cooperation with industry) and program 5 (training of the unemployed) soaked up $100 million. For this figure, the government claims some 200,000 Canadians participated in one way or another. But there is little to show what their participation achieved. The dropout rate may be as high as 60%, and the profitability to those who completed the courses is practically unknown.
I do not know whether these strong words are correct, and perhaps the minister, in replying, can say whether he takes exception to that statement published in the Monetary Times. Such a statement implants a nagging doubt that can be resolved better by an *examination in the more intimate setting of a committee of the house than by an examination in this awesome forum.
I continue quoting from the article:
Even Ontario, which made greater use of the funds than all other provinces combined, heard its own economic council report:	"Program 5
lacks well-defined objectives at all levels of its operations: federal, provincial and local. The lack of objectives complicates the development of effective policies and the use of meaningful performance measures. (Its role) has not been defined and continued procrastination could result in a training program for the unemployed which diverges widely from the nation's and the province's real needs."

I was pleased to hear the minister announce that he would broaden the statistical operations that support the manpower program. Admittedly he spoke in the other language of Canada, and while we have excellent translation facilities one cannot always catch what is being said. If one is too close to the minister he hears him speaking in his original language, which is distracting; and if one is too far away he can hear a buzz coming from behind the curtains, which is distracting, too. I gather the minister said that the statistical information so far available to him and his officials was incomplete and that new statistical devices were to be employed. This is wise.

In the March, 1967, issue of the Canadian Statistical Review a feature article on Canadian manpower statistics supports the need for more and different types of information with respect to unemployment in Canada. There is the labour force survey taken from 35,000 households. It is a national survey, a sort of spot check here and there, but does not examine the problem in detail. As the article I have just referred to says on page 3 of the publication:
For those in the labour force with a job, some qualitative information is available regarding their industrial and occupational attachment within broad groupings. Similarly, for the unemployed the number of weeks seeking work is recorded.
