The article, in speaking of administrative records, says that those records are deficient and are limited in usefulness as economic statistics. I am glad to see the minister coming to grips with this problem.
I should like to know about that. Again, I think a committee approach, where one could call in experts and deal with this new type of statistical approach, would be helpful. While the minister can be very frank with us and give certain answers, he is perhaps just filling in Hansard and we are occupying ourselves with technical information that is of interest to only a relatively small number of members.
On the question of immigration, Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank the minister for taking, in the Halifax area, a step that has been long overdue. After consultation with the Department of Transport and some urging from Halifax members and the port of Halifax commission, the minister has now corrected the problem. In the past when groups of, say, below 250 immigrants arrived in Halifax it was not feasible to arrange special trains for them, and frequently while awaiting the regular service they had to hang around the immigration sheds. * This represented a rather bleak welcome to their new country. Instead of the red carpet that was promised in Rome, say, they found these cold and somewhat institutional rooms of very poor comfort. This was their first impression, quite apart from their arrival in the beautiful harbour of Halifax, upon landing in this country.
3542	COMMONS
Supply-Manpower and Immigration
The minister has solved this problem by making hotel accommodation in Halifax available to these groups of newcomers to Canada. I should like to put this on the public record. People who are not able to board special trains immediately are provided with hotel accommodation. This was a very humane and very reasonable step, which I presume will be applied in other parts of Canada.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, we have had some discussion today about the ten-point system. The hon. member for Greenwood and the hon. member for St. Paul's wondered how well they would qualify and what criteria would be used. They wondered whether you can judge a man accurately by looking him in the eye. My suggestion is-and this method can be used to test any person, particularly somebody who asks you to endorse his note-that the test should be: Would you buy a used car from this person? I throw that suggestion out as a swift alternative to the laborious setting down and totalling of points. However, I do have reservations about the test I have suggested. I am afraid that were it applied completely it might mean that Canada would become occupied by little old ladies, of both sexes, who drove their vehicles only on Sunday.

Mr. Chairman, the minister expressed his optimism tonight and hoped that Canada would have one of the best manpower policies in the world. We all agree that this is what we would like to have in this country. However, I do not think we are as close to achieving that desired result as the minister seems to think.
I believe there is little cause for comfort in the progress of the manpower department. Many of the problems of that department are beyond the ability of the minister to solve. I think this has to be stated. I should also like to say that a couple of weeks ago I brought some matters to the minister's attention and was very pleased when he rose at the end of my comments and put some forthright statements on the record for the guidance of people in offices across this country.
We know that the minister has failed to attract the necessary personnel to his department. We understand this is a general problem and applies not only to his department but to others. I believe the minister has tried to attract these personnel and I hope that before this debate concludes he will tell us frankly what are the difficulties and what

solutions he has in mind for correcting the problem.
It is also fairly obvious that the minister has had to change his plans with regard to making payments under some of the programs, because of the difficulties encountered at the federal-provincial level, in terms of defining the jurisdiction of the federal government as opposed to that of the provincial governments. Until the government finds a better solution than has appeared up to this time, the whole program will be bedevilled by these strange situations that cannot be corrected and which cause enormous inconvenience to people seeking retraining in this country.
I hope that my remarks tonight will be somewhat more rational than those of the leader of the official opposition. The hon. member for Ontario began by criticizing the minister for his failure to provide enough money for retraining programs. The hon. member said that the absence of funds in this area resulted in the exclusion of people from retraining programs. He then concluded his speech by taking the government to task for spending too much money and for not reducing the tax load on the citizens of this country. I suggest there is room for legitimate criticism in this regard; but this was not that kind of criticism. I believe that the kind of criticism in which the pot calls the kettle black does not help us in the course of trying to solve these problems.
When members of the opposition, whose record while in office contains, amongst other things, a history of the highest unemployment rate in this country for many years, rise and criticize the government for the present level of unemployment, some questions have to be raised. I believe the problem of unemployment is of paramount importance and it is the chief point with which I should like to deal tonight. Before doing so, however, I should like to point out the third difficulty in the minister's department that has not been adequately explained.
I believe the department has been excessively cautious from the commencement of the program to the present time. If we consider the mobility program, for example, we have seen it revised from one stage to another. It started out with loans and grants and has now progressed-I might say, favourably progressed-to a structure of grants and has got away from loans.
October 26, 1967	COMMONS
From the inception of this program we have pointed out the difficulty of a proposition which included loans and grants. We have now progressed to the grants stage in the program. We have not, however, reached the stage of a clearcut understanding that the grants must be substantially higher than those now proposed by the minister.
The hardcore unemployment in certain areas of this country points up the need for mobility in those areas. The reason people have to be moved from certain communities is not that of individual unemployment, the kind of individual unemployment that occurs in an area that has diversified industry. It results from a complete shutdown of an industry, from the obsolescence of an activity, and it means that the working community suffers greatly. One of the chief obstacles in moving people in a situation of that type is that to move them from the surroundings in which they have become accustomed to living means that they lose everything they have worked for all their lives.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Usually it means the loss of a home. If the community is on its way out and there is no opportunity to sell that home, even giving people an extra $500 under their allowances is not an adequate compensation. The department will have to consider compensating losses of this type in the same way in which society generally has to do it when it expropriates land for the purpose of building a highway or an expressway. It is not enough to say: We will give you something toward your future. That "something" does not go very far. Since the dislocation is part of the over-all price that society pays for change and progress, that price should not have to be paid for only by the victims upon whose shoulders the dislocation falls. The remedy is a house for a house. This should be obvious to hon. members in the opposition.
I have seen people in my own riding being forced to migrate from their homes and the homes of their ancestors, after the most productive years of their life have been spent, and having to start out in new surroundings where, generally speaking, housing is difficult to obtain, at a time when the money they have received does not go very far, and when much of the furniture they have acquired is either no longer useful or too costly to move. What they need is an adequate opportunity for resettlement, and that cost should be borne by society generally rather than by these people in particular. If a mobility program is to adequately reflect the needs of this

Supply-Manpower and Immigration country, then this is the position that we must take.
It seems that the minister is frequently put in the position of a painter who has to cover the defects of the carpenters who are building the structure in this country. I should like to suggest to the minister that, like any other painter, he could camouflage some of the minor flaws, but if he wishes to preserve his reputation he had better talk to the carpenters and review the structure because there is a limit to what even painting can do.
The threatened closing down of Dosco is an example of the sort of thing I am talking about. Here is an industry which decides on its own and for its own reasons, without regard for the disruption that it creates in the community, to cease operations. The minister of manpower is left to pick up the pieces and to try to patch up the job or paint it over to make it look good. The real failure in this case is the failure of the government to have anticipated this problem and to have done some structural work before the roof fell in. Apparently the minister recognized this, and in the Globe and Mail of October 17 he is reported to have said the following:
-Change is inevitable in a dynamic economy, but corporations have to accept their responsibilities to the communities in which they operate... and legislation may be needed to enforce the point.
I suggest to him that it is not that legislation may be needed, but that legislation is needed. I would like to hear from the minister as to what he intends to propose to the government by way of legislation to prevent Dosco from abdicating its responsibility, and what he proposes to do about other similar situations.
We may have reached the point where we will start hearing proposals from Liberals and Conservatives to nationalize Dosco. Certainly such proposals have already been made by my own party. I think there is a great danger in such a proposal. It seems that the only time when nationalization is proposed is when the particular industry has collapsed and it becomes the only way to preserve some of the social and human elements involved. In time people will forget about the irresponsibility of the company and will only remember the difficulties it had in operating, and then blame nationalization for what is essentially a fault of the government in not having anticipated the situation.
There was a time when Dosco should have been nationalized, and in the last 10 or 15 years that suggestion has been made to successive governments. However, it was

Supply-Manpower and Immigration always pooh-poohed. Right until the last minute the impression was left that the people in Cape Breton were in no danger and there was no need for the government to step into the picture. That optimism has not been borne out and a serious crisis is facing Nova Scotia. Referring to the labour government in Britain will not absolve the government of this country from its failure to live up to its responsibilities, for its camouflaging of the circumstances and for waiting until disaster strikes. The government will not impress the people in Cape Breton by muttering about the labour government in Great Britain.
I should now like to speak about some of my own personal experiences and observations as the representative of the riding of Waterloo South. We have a unique riding in the sense that there is a tremendous diversity of industry in our area, all the way from textiles to machinery. It has been instructive to observe what has happened over a period of years. The experience in the riding has convinced me of the tremendous urgency and need for a manpower policy, and this is why I have been such a strong advocate of the upgrading of training and of generally increasing the level of skills to meet the growing needs of an industrial society. However, one conclusion that must be reached when examining the manpower policies is that no manpower policy can be successful unless the minister insists on an economy of full employment. A year and a half ago when the employment situation was better than it is today I had the opportunity to see how readily manpower programs were instituted. Today we find our older workers cannot find employment and people who want to work cannot find work because of their age. We find that part-time female workers cannot find employment, young men out of high school are also in this position and immigrants from abroad as well as people from other provinces who have moved into the riding are experiencing difficulties in obtaining employment. This was not the case when the level of employment was higher. When industry needed workers there was no obstacle to developing special programs for women who wanted to work part time. Immigrants could be absorbed readily and so could people from other parts of Canada.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
The minute you get some unemployment, some people are classified as unemployable or only partially employable. Then, the old problems that have faced this country for many

years come to the fore. We hear statements from the Minister of Finance, when he expresses concern over inflation, to the effect that something has to be done to take the heat off. The implication in many of the minister's speeches is that we must increase the level of unemployment in this country. I urge the minister of manpower, as a person who knows what unemployment means to the ordinary man, to use all his influence within the cabinet to make certain that this kind of policy does not prevail. Other solutions have to be found to control inflation in Canada. The solution of creating more unemployment is totally unacceptable to our society.
The solution of increased supply is one that should be sought. We have many opportunities for increasing efficiency and productivity of our industry. The solution to this problem is not the sole responsibility of the minister of manpower, but he should use his influence within the cabinet to make sure that the approach of increasing supply and productivity is the one that is pursued, rather than the suggestion that a little unemployment is the answer to our economic ills. Before this debate is concluded, I hope the minister will indicate his position on this question. I see some consultation is taking place between the two ministers in question. I feel that the country deserves an answer from the minister of manpower. He should tell us where he stands on this particular issue, and which position he will support.
We all believe in the programs that are being suggested, such as the mobility program, retraining programs, increased market information, better placement service, improved provincial planning and increased aid to education. All of these things are of the greatest importance. However, they are effects rather than causes. We should never lose sight of the fact that under full employment, even in the absence of a directed program, most of the essentials of this manpower policy find expression.
There is mobility in spite of inadequate government measures. The unemployed in one part of the country find that there are job openings elsewhere. The word does not always come through government agencies but often results from visits back home or through previous migrants. Training takes place in plants that previously refused to consider such programs, once the pool of skilled labour dries up. Individuals who were considered unemployable by reason of age or lack of skill, suddenly become useful when
October 26, 1967	COMMONS
the cream is skimmed off the labour market. The hard core cases no longer seem to be such hard cores. Unemployment amongst the young ceases to be a crisis. Admittedly, a planned manpower program would speed up this process by making the way easier for both management and labour, and for that reason it should be aggressively pursued. Good manpower programs would also do the research and set up the machinery to overcome the guessing and uncertainty of the grapevine. For these reasons, we are all in favour of manpower policies. I would conclude by pointing out to the minister that all of this is conditional and dependant on the philosophy of full employment.

I will just mention that from the year 1961 to the year 1967 the number of immigrants to this country increased from 72,000 to over 200,000.
The hon. member for Carleton, a former minister of immigration, expressed some concern at the number of agricultural workers who are brought into Canada. I can appreciate that concern. Until there is some change in the economy of our agriculture sector, which of course is one of our more important industries, I am afraid that the agricultural workers brought to this country will soon drift to the urban areas, to which many of our own citizens are going. One interesting statistic indicates that we had 195,000 immigrants in 1966, about half of which were classified as workers and the other half as dependants. One quarter of the working category were classified as professional and technical people.
We need a great many more people in this country in order to develop our true potential. Canada, of course, is a land of opportunity with a land mass slightly larger than the United States of America to the south of us, but with only one tenth of its population. I am reminded of a highly industrialized midEuropean country from which many people come to my area, which is not as large as our

In spite of the points system, which has been criticized by members of the opposition, the new regulations will certainly provide uniformity in the consideration of immigrants from all over the world, and provide what I am sure this government wants to provide, an opportunity for more people to come to Canada. I have met Mr. Peterson, Mr. Chairman, and had I been an immigration officer-I do not class myself as trained in this connection-I would probably have accepted him. Unfortunately, under the new regulations he did not qualify. I understand that as of this week formal notification has been sent to him that he should leave the country. However, he may

Supply-Manpower and Immigration take his case to an inquiry officer and, following that, if necessary to the immigration appeal board.
Although I support the regulations, Mr. Chairman, I feel-and I think the members of the committee on immigration felt much the same way-that compassionate cases, or cases involving exceptional circumstances, should be considered by this enlarged appeal board. I say this because I am sure he is the type of citizen we want here.
Just a word about the manpower program, Mr. Chairman. Many problems have arisen in the implementation of this program, the federal government having accepted responsibility for 100 per cent of the cost. I think no area has had more problems than my constituency of Waterloo North, most of them surprisingly enough in the urban centres of Kitchener and Waterloo.

Under the old shared cost program between the provincial and federal governments new facilities have been provided and the staff has been increased. The program has also been enlarged. As a matter of fact, almost three months before the changeover took place on April 1 last it was indicated to me that there was some concern over the apparent proliferation of activity under the program. I realize members of the opposition have placed on record statistics relating to the lack of trainees under this program, and I also realize it is highly desirable for every citizen of Canada to take part in the program, should they desire to improve their education or training. Nevertheless I feel there must be some control even if all who can benefit themselves and upgrade their skills are given every opportunity to do so.
I do not share the concern which has been registered this evening about the three year restriction on school drop-outs and hippies. In many of these cases there is lack of motivation. I think the provincial departments of education should accept responsibility here. I am sure that some of these people would benefit if they worked for several years and developed a desire which would motivate them to undertake some form of training.
I have one suggestion to make to the minister which I would ask him to consider seriously. Under the present regulations I do not think consideration is given to women recently widowed and with dependants and who, because they have not previously been members of the labour force, are not able to receive the training they can certainly use in order to provide for themselves and their families. Mr. Chairman, as far as the estimates of the Department of Manpower and Immigration are concerned, I have some remarks which may not be more brilliant than those which have been made until now but which at least will offer the advantage of not being politically inspired, remarks with no other meaning than: "Because we are Conservatives, we could do better than you; or because we are Liberals, we are doing better than you."
This afternoon, I was among those who felt admiration for the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) who seems to be a brilliant criminal lawyer. If ever I were to seriously break the law out west, I would call on his services, because he seems exceedingly brilliant when he speaks on legal or criminal matters. But when he is being

Supply-Manpower and Immigration influenced by political partisanship, he is less brilliant, Mr. Chairman. In fact, this afternoon, he gave a speech which, to my mind, settled nothing. He said this: The Canadian Pacific wants to eliminate from Calgary certain operations involving the lay-off of 300 or 400 employees.
I should like to remind the hon. member for Bow River that the city of Winnipeg also at one time complained when Air Canada wanted to remove some of their operations. The city of Montreal could complain at this time that Bell Telephone will be moving 350 or 400 employees to Ottawa. My own city could complain that some operations have to be moved elsewhere.
Mr. Chairman, the basic problem is not the fact that industries must move, but if we go to the bottom of things, the problem is that we are entering the age of automation, and as a result we must realize that we cannot expect industries to continue their operations and meet their expenses unless they submit to the requirements of this age of automation.
I say to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration that his program is a good one; it is an excellent one in the circumstances and it is not his fault if it is ten or fifteen years too late, but I feel he should arrange for studies to be made about the situation of the labour market and of the Canadian economy in the next thirty or thirty-five years.
I know that the Americans have been able to establish committees which attempt to anticipate our mode of life in twenty, twenty-five, thirty or thirty-five years from now. We are told that in the year 2000, hardly more than 20 or 25 per cent of the people will be employed during a reasonable part of the day. If the present rate is maintained, automation will intensify and this is what should already be anticipated.
Complaining about the Canadian Pacific or Air Canada, or my complaining because enterprises must move out of my town to meet the demands of automation, this does not solve the problem itself. We are merely applying poultices, trying to solve the problem partially; and we have to start all over again the next morning.
I want the minister to understand that I am not saying this to criticize his policy, because what he is doing is immeasurably better than what we have known in many a year; nor do I want to seem to play politics. I feel that if the Conservatives were in power they would probably be doing the same
3548	COMMONS
Supply-Manpower and Immigration thing, because it is a necessity in this day and age. But unfortunately, the parties in power never manage to put the poultice on the sore before it festers and becomes almost incurable, whereas they should anticipate 10, 15, 20 or 25 years ahead of time and adopt such measures as would keep the situation from becoming so serious.
Nevertheless, I congratulate the minister because I can tell him, on the basis of my personal experience, the experience in my own riding, that our manpower office, with an establishment of about thirty or thirty-five experts, works marvels in difficult circumstances, even though the legislation has just been implemented. I would like to quote some names and the testimony of people who took advantage of its services, and who tell us that the legislation initiated and implemented by him is in the van and gives good results. It would probably be indiscreet to go too far in that field. Nevertheless, I want to congratulate him.
I will repeat also, Mr. Chairman, a thing that I already told the minister. I do not say it to his address but rather to others. I think he is being saddled with too many responsibilities. They would be enough to keep busy a minister of immigration, a minister of manpower and possibly a leader of the Liberal party in Quebec.
I wonder if this habit of putting a crushing burden on a man is not destroying leaders who could give their full measure in another field, but who are expected to give it in three completely unrelated fields with the result that unfortunate things happen, as we have found out. There comes a time when this affects their health; we lose those men and they have to be replaced and others have to be initiated with all the inherent delays, and their loss is to be regretted.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
I mention this again, hoping that those whose task it is to choose the leaders know how to divide responsibilities. In saying that,
I do not doubt the talent and capability of the hon. Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand). I have seen him work with the labour unions for such a long time that I am well aware of his extraordinary vitality.
I know that his responsibilities have just been increased a thousandfold. Knowing him,
I know that he, too, would like to excel in his work, but one cannot do so when one is trying to do three things at once. I mention this, because I think it is the sort of thing

DEBATES	October 26, 1967
which only an independent member can mention in committee.
As I said before, the basic problem we are discussing concerns manpower retraining and vocational training, which must be undertaken in the light of the era of great automation in which we are entering. Already in five or ten years excessive automation will make it difficult to find employment for our people, and studies made by the Americans in particular show that in the year 2000, which is not so very far away, only about thirty years from now, only 20 or 25 per cent of the population will be reasonably employed. What will other people do then? A department of recreation and a department of idleness will have to be set up, because all those people cannot be left to starve to death as a result of automation taking their jobs away from them.
For the time being, Mr. Chairman, after listening to all the speeches made this afternoon, and in which there always is something worth remembering-and when I rise to ask the floor, I would not think for a moment that my words could be any better than anybody else's, perhaps just as good but not better-I simply would not want to repeat everything that has been said here, and well said at that. However, I should like to forget the partisan views expressed by the Conservatives when they say: If we had been in your shoes, we would have done a better job; and then the Liberals reply: When you were there, you were unable to do any better.
I am a believer in historical development, and if today I can enjoy television, drive a car, and things like that which were unavailable in my father's and grand-father's time, it is precisely because historical evolution and progress occur independently of us and shall continue to do so.
All we ask from those who have responsibilities, is to do what they can. I think that the Tories, when they were in power, did whatever they could under the circumstances, with the means at their disposal, and I think that the same can be said of this Liberal government. I should like my remarks to be constructive, rather than necessarily destructive, because my personal aim is not to overthrow the government. It is simply to offer my co-operation, so that the duly formed and democratically elected government may under the present circumstances, act in the public interest and provide for all as much of the good things of this world as possible. This is the justification for my remarks.
October 26, 1967

I will say to the minister, as I have already done, that I feel it would be advisable to give specal directives to the department of manpower to make sure that the so-called old people-that is over 40-may, if they are still in good health, find some employment, or they should be taken care of some way or another.
Now, the minister knows, because he has worked in the labour movement, that over 40 or 45 years of age, it is extremely difficult to find employment due to the requirements of collective bargaining, group insurance and many others, and that Canadians are doomed to idleness despite the fact they could increase the productivity of the country, because they have acquired over the years an experience which helps them to produce more efficiently than younger workers and thereby contributes to the national production. I feel we do not take good enough care of our old people, and one is old at an early age these days. Every week, not only in my riding, but in surrounding ridings, people tell me that at 40, 42, 45, they are too old to work. To my mind, there should be a special section in the department of manpower to deal with the so-called old people. I say that there are old people who, at 65, are much younger than many others, because their morale is good, their health is good, and they could help to increase national productivity instead of becoming a burden on public funds and being condemned to the demoralizing idleness to which they are doomed under our present system.
I repeat to the minister that I want my criticism to be constructive. He has already gone a long way towards improving working conditions, and my remarks are not intended to criticize his administration.
I should like also to repeat a suggestion I addressed very briefly yesterday to the minister of forestry (Mr. Sauve). I say "briefly" because, as everyone, I had to limit myself to twenty minutes, and as I had been relegated to the end of the list, at the last moment, I was asked to co-operate and limit my remarks to two minutes, and I did so.
I told the minister of forestry, and I repeat it to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand), that there should be in the department of manpower a special section to deal with young people still in school and who could work during their two or three months' holidays to pay part of their tuition.

I was saying that a special program, perhaps a widespread reforestation program or something of the kind should be set up; that would be to the benefit of the country and it would also reduced overcrowding in the plants, make room for others and also reduce the budget for scholarships and costs guaranteed by the government. On the other hand, those young people might derive from it an education and salutary discipline.
I feel that in co-operation with his colleagues, the minister should study the possibility of introducing a bill so that all those young people still in school-I am talking about those at the secondary and university level mainly, young people of 18, 19, 20, 21 and over-would be assured of getting a job and an income, without swelling the labour market, and at the same time some discipline.
I would not call that military service. We could give it all kinds of names but if the government intends to set up a similar system, it would not involve much more expenditures since it is already obliged to meet certain needs by various means, such as scholarships and others. Furthermore, it might relieve the labour market.
Earlier, someone talked about woman-power which is too often neglected. When I refer to womanpower, I mean the widows, for instance, who still have children to raise; the wives whose heartless husbands have deserted them without paying them alimony; the ladies who may still be young at heart but not so young in years, who must provide for their maintenance. A special division in the manpower department must be set up for them so that they may earn an honest living, and have a place where they can find out what benefits are available to them, what social legislation has been set up so that they would not have, as it is the case now, to go and fish for themselves, if I may use that term, to avail themselves of all the opportunities of the legislation.
This brings me to repeat another suggestion I made to the minister the other day to the effect that courses in human relations should be taken by all public servants, federal, provincial, municipal and others, who get up one fine morning and think themselves miniature potentates oblivious to everything that is going on in the world and who treat their customers, who are the taxpayers, the citizens who pay taxes, with unmitigated cynicism. I do not say this situation is general but it exists and they probably become blase by hearing so many problems. But the problems exist just the same, and they should
3550	COMMONS
Supply-Manpower and Immigration learn what is being taught to employees of private enterprise. They know that if they do not deal properly with the customers, the latter will patronize rival stores.
This does not exist in the public service, but nevertheless, the public servant should be constantly reminded, once or twice a year, that he is dealing with human beings who, after all, are not his servants but his employers, since they pay taxes, since they vote on election day and since they are kings on that particular day, that he must treat them with every possible consideration and not wait until they inquire about all the possibilities of the legislation, in short, that he is being paid by the government to put all his knowledge at the disposal of taxpayers in order to acquaint them with the legislation and help them solve their problems.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
I say it is not current enough and, once more, this is no reflection on the minister. I am merely making constructive suggestions. Lectures on public relations should be regularly given not every five years but every year and as often as necessary. Experts should check the way the employees of these offices manage their work; it must be borne in mind that they are dealing with human beings endowed with sensitiveness, with a soul, with personal and family problems and who deserve all the consideration that the public servant should give those who help pay his salary, who elect the people who will decide when he is going to be employed in the service of the community.
Mr. Chairman, this afternoon, mention was made that it was perhaps not reasonable to require that a candidate be out of school for three years. I think that, as in everything else, there are arguments for and against. Of course, I know that manpower services cannot empty schools to absorb the students, but I wonder if it might not be possible to find a compromise, because there are special cases. For instance, I am thinking of a case I witnessed back home: a boy had to leave school to help his widowed mother take care of the family. After working a few months, he became unemployed. He could not avail himself of the services the manpower offices offer ordinary unemployed. If he could then he should have been told.
I see that the minister is protesting and I am happy to hear him protest because I will call someone to order. Someone in the office should think of human relations and tell

DEBATES	October 26, 1967
him: My friend, you are entitled to such and such a thing. Do not compel him to come three or four times to the member's office to say: I went to the manpower centre but without success because I have been out of school less than three years. I repeat my suggestion about human relations.
As far as naturalization after five years is concerned, that is clearly questionable; there are pros and cons. I imagine that the immigrant who is here, even though he is not naturalized after one, two or three years, has all the privileges enjoyed by Canadians, except perhaps that of voting; he can wait three or perhaps four years, that is immaterial, that is not too serious.
French immigration was discussed; that is another problem. It must be understood that, in general, French-speaking people are not prone to emigrate. I think that the minister will not contest that statement.
It should also be said that the province of Quebec is not organized to welcome Frenchspeaking people. I should like to illustrate my point with two cases. The hon. minister will forgive me for using them as examples but I think they are typical.
Some months ago I received in my office a young French immigrant, an orphan who had all sorts of problems. I do not intend to tell his story; suffice it to say that he managed to get into the country. He has been unemployed since then.
In his own country, he had studied what we call mechanics-he worked on precision machines-then he came to Canada and, for some reason or other, the immigration service was unable to find him a job in his line of work. I wonder how he managed to get into the country. At one point, he was given a job as stone mason. He went to work as a bricklayer but he is only so high. He is shorter and thinner than the minister. Think of it. He did not last a day; the contractor fired him. That is obvious. Then the immigration and manpower office found him a job as a welder; he went to work as a welder, but he did not last half a day. He was not a welder.
He is living in dire poverty and he came to my office to tell me so. That is a typical case, Mr. Chairman. He said to me: Listen, I would very much like to work, but this is my trade; I studied at home and that is all I know. I cannot carry cement or cinder blocks on my shoulders, because I am a little over 4 feet tall and I weigh barely 100 pounds. I would not mind working as a welder, but I am not trained for that and I cannot keep a job.
October 26, 1967	COMMONS
Therefore, there is something lacking in the immigration service.
I want to talk about another case the minister is aware of, as I received a letter from him today; as it is neither personal nor confidential, I can quote it. It is the case of a man from Haiti who came here and took training as an electrician. As everyone knows, to obtain an electrician's license in Quebec, a period of six months training as an apprentice is required. As he is being refused a working permit by immigration, he cannot get his six months apprenticeship permit.
Mr. Chairman, I repeat to the minister that I am not blaming him for this, but some officials who know nothing about human relations. As far as I know, this boy has now been waiting for six months to be allowed to complete his apprenticeship and get his certificate; after that, he is perhaps ready to pack up and go back home, but nevertheless he cannot get permission to work. There is an employer who would like to hire him; in fact, out of kindness, he has paid for his studies. While they lasted, he had to follow a crash course, and because of red tape or bureaucracy, he was unable to work. Now he is inactive, idle, and lives on hand-outs from social agencies. Then I say to myself: there is something wrong somewhere.
Mr. Chairman, as I said, the minister is the last person to whom I would direct destructive criticism, even to whom I would inflict sorrow, for I am greatly impressed with the tremendous amount of work that he does. However, I do mention these things, which probably escape his attention, because I am aware he has too many responsibilities to shoulder.
He has been given the responsibilities of three departments. Amazingly enough, he has assumed them up to now without weakening, but I think some day his burden will have to be eased, so that he can show what he is capable of doing and know what is going on in all his departments.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to raise another matter, but since I am the first to object when a member speaks one minute beyond the time allotted to him and since I insist on the right to speak for myself and for the others as well, I shall be brief. I find the manpower program, under its present form, an excellent one, at least in the present circumstances. Nevertheless, some thought should be given right now to the fact that within the next five, ten, fifteen or twenty years, we shall be facing an excessive automation which will bring about the lay-off of a
DEBATES	3551
Supply-Manpower and Immigration great number of workers quite willing to work. The problem will not be settled by saying that the Canadian Pacific has laid off 300 workers, that Dosco has laid off 1,000 others, that Air Canada has dismissed so many and some other company so many. Let us prepare for the coming age of automation-whether we like it or not-and let us try to provide for some legislation which will enable everyone to earn a living some way or other, or else, let us find a means to enable the people to live, although unemployed, if things should come to that. That is where there should be set up organizations likely to anticipate what will happen in the country within the next twenty, twenty-five or thirty years.
If we wait for unemployment to become general, for the sore to fester, it will be too late, Mr. Chairman. We will be putting poultices to relieve the sore, as we are doing with manpower; poultices are being applied and have good results and that is fortunate, because otherwise the situation would be much worse. But we are not reaching the root of the problem.

maintopic: INCOME TAX-REQUEST FOR FORGIVENESS OF INTEREST ON TAX ARREARS OF PENSIONERS
INCOME TAX-REQUEST FOR FORGIVENESS OF INTEREST ON TAX ARREARS OF PENSIONERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, back in 1966 a number of people in the country were rather surprised to find notices in their mail boxes from the Department of National Revenue asking them to pay interest on overdue installments of income tax. It is true that the interest requested was in most cases not large, $1.50, $2 or $3, but in spite of the small amounts in question these notices caused a great deal of concern to the people who received them. In most cases these people are retired and their only income apart from their old age security pension is some modest amount of interest from government bonds or from a bank account. Obviously people on limited incomes feel that even an additional expenditure of 
DEBATES	October 26. 1967
$2 or $3 could better be used for their own purposes than placed in the hands of the friendly tax collector. At the same time many felt rather disconcerted that somehow or other they were now expected to pay tax in instalments, when they never had to do so throughout their working lives and when they did not receive adequate notice or, in the case of some, did not receive any notice at all of the department's view that they should pay tax in a different manner.
It would appear, possibly because of the department's new computer which I hope is the servant of the department rather than its master, it was easier to determine exactly who would come within the provisions of section 49 of the act. Under it if people receive no income or only a limited amount of income from employment, they are supposed to pay their tax in instalments. I believe this provision was originally intended to apply mainly to people in the professional class or to those with large investments. Perhaps because of the greater efficiency of the administrative forces of the department, people in a much different income category were now found technically to be in the class of people who were supposed to pay their tax in instalments.
I, and I suppose other members as well, wrote to the minister on behalf of a number of people in this group, pointing out that this created a number of difficulties for these people. They would have to pay these additional amounts in interest if they did not pay the tax in instalments. Many of these people were advanced in years and had various infirmities which would make it difficult to make out forms four times a year and to estimate the tax and some of them were able to have only a limited amount of education. They were all accustomed to having the tax deducted at the source by their employers and filling in a form once a year and then paying any balance owing.
As I say, I pointed out to the minister in corresponding with him on behalf of a number of these citizens, the hardships created because if these people did not pay their tax in instalments they would be liable for interest. If they attempted to comply with the regulations, they would have all the difficulties of filling out or finding someone to help them fill out the forms. These are people who have spent all their lives helping to build up this country. They should be spared this hardship if at all possible.
October 26, 1967

The year is drawing to a close and the time tor settling up accounts with the Department of National Revenue will soon be upon us once more. I felt this question was of sufficient urgency that I could bring this matter up in this adjournment debate. I ask the minister if he will not see if something can be done for the people in the category I have mentioned. They are mainly retired people who have a very limited income, even taking into account this interest in addition to their pension. I hope the minister can help relieve these people of this burden. I have had the response made to me by the department: Well, if this was not done the people could rearrange the way they get their income and avoid paying the tax in the year in which it is due.
In most cases, this does not apply to the group in question. I believe Canada savings bond interest is payable only in the fall, and this procedure cannot be changed. Yet the people with this type of limited income to which I have referred are asked to pay taxes in instalments before this interest is due. In conclusion, I ask the minister to take action to help the people in question by removing this burden from them.

Since I became Minister of National Revenue, this has been a very perplexing problem. I think that the requirement that people pay income tax in instalments when they have income from sources other than salary is a very fair provision of the act. The ordinary person who is working for a salary has his tax deducted monthly. This parliament put into the Income Tax Act a provision whereby other people had to pay quarterly, which is a little less onerous than the provision applying to a person earning a salary who has his tax deducted monthly, a (10:10 p.m.)
In the past, because of the difficulty of computing interest, since it required four computations in order to determine the interest payable by one person in a year, small amounts of interest were overlooked by the department merely as an administrative matter. I may say I am very pleased we have a computer in the Department of National Revenue dealing with personal income tax returns because we process them faster and we save the government of Canada a large amount of money every year. I could quote figures that indicate that 10 or 12 years ago it cost $2.08 per $100 to collect it, and that the cost is now 27053-225
DEBATES	3555
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion down to something like 96 cents. Nevertheless I have been worried about people who were on a salary, who retire, and then start to receive the old age pension and find themselves suddenly charged $2, $3 or $4 interest.
As a result of this, during the last year I have had a study made in my department of this question, and we have come to the conclusion that the cost of collecting-that is to say, the cost of putting out the information, submitting the bill to the taxpayers, collecting the money, following it up, writing letters and answering inquiries-is not worth the amount of tax that is collected. In other words, it costs more to collect these small amounts than is warranted by the amount of revenue that is received by the crown.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I have decided, and I hope parliament will support me-and if I recall correctly the last time my estimates were before the house for consideration, I am sure all hon. members will support me-that we will take action in order to eliminate interest charges of under $5 to the taxpayers of Canada. This means that ordinarily a person with a small income who starts receiving the old age pension but fails to remit the instalments in the first year, even though we have given him warning in his first old age pension cheque that the cheque will be subject to tax, will not have to worry about this in the future. I think that by imposing this $5 limit most of the urgent cases will be taken care of.
